summary: Manual review after a burst of athlete-facing work (2026-10-02 to 10-05): sleep debt, ride fuelling, protein tick, personal best wall with FTP estimate, pre-session brief, what-worked memory, return-to-run tracker, life-load tags, minimum viable week, two-minute downshift and the just check command. Marked six catalog ideas Done (structured .zwo workouts, volume trend alert, morning check-in, return-to-run tracker, dependable project checks, test-free FTP estimate). Added six athlete-facing proposals that do not overlap built or catalogued work. Source/documentation review only; no tests, syncs or model calls were run.

ideas.title: One trustworthy check before shipping
ideas.problem: Frontend behavior tests exist without an npm test command. The backend test command depends on a local dependency folder and mixed import roots. Some tests also use dates that age out of the period they query.
ideas.proposal: Create a documented project check command that runs frontend behavior tests, the frontend build, and backend tests in a reproducible environment. Repair confirmed fixture and clock assumptions without weakening behavior assertions.
ideas.benefit: Make every new feature faster to verify and catch regressions before they reach your training workflow.
acceptance_criteria: One documented command runs the relevant frontend and backend checks from a fresh dependency environment.
Tests do not fail merely because today's date changes.
Strength comparison fixtures include the schema the production code needs.
Existing failing assertions are investigated; no tests are deleted or weakened to obtain a passing run.

ideas.title: Pick up where you left off in Data & Sync
ideas.problem: The selected source on Data & Sync is kept only in component state. Opening a link or refreshing returns to Strava even when you were reviewing another source.
ideas.proposal: Keep the active source in a validated URL query parameter. Preserve it across refresh and browser navigation, and make direct links to Apple Health, HealthFit, and Fitbod work.
ideas.benefit: Return directly to the import source you were working on and share precise troubleshooting links.
acceptance_criteria: A direct URL can select any of the four existing source panels.
Refresh and browser Back/Forward restore the selected source.
Unknown source values fall back safely to Strava.
Switching panels never starts an import.

ideas.title: A smoother dashboard without a mouse
ideas.problem: The app shell provides a main landmark, while Data & Sync nests another main inside it. Repeated navigation and unclear landmark structure add friction for keyboard and screen-reader users.
ideas.proposal: Audit the app shell and page wrappers for a single main landmark, add a visible-on-focus skip-to-content link, and check focus placement after route changes. Keep the current visual design.
ideas.benefit: Make the dashboard easier to navigate with a keyboard and clearer for assistive technology.
acceptance_criteria: Each route exposes exactly one main landmark.
The first keyboard shortcut target is a usable skip-to-content link.
Visible focus remains clear on desktop and mobile layouts.
A browser smoke check covers keyboard navigation on Dashboard and Data & Sync.

ideas.title: Keep unfinished set entries when you switch away
ideas.problem: The live strength runner stores reps and weight in component state until Log set succeeds. syncInputs replaces those inputs from saved or target values when the current set changes or the session reloads, so an unfinished entry can disappear after switching exercises or refreshing. Completed-set persistence does not cover this draft state.
ideas.proposal: Keep a small local draft keyed by workout and set ID for unsubmitted reps and weight. Restore it when returning to the same active set, clearly label it as not logged, and offer an explicit discard action. Reconcile drafts with the latest server state before restoring so another tab or a completed workout cannot silently be overwritten. Keep the existing Log set action as the only completion step.
ideas.benefit: Avoid retyping or forgetting the reps and load you just entered when you check another exercise or accidentally refresh mid-workout.
evidence: frontend/src/views/StrengthWorkoutSession.vue: syncInputs and currentSet watcher replace unsaved input values
frontend/src/views/StrengthWorkoutSession.vue: changePosition calls syncInputs after changing the current exercise/set
frontend/src/views/StrengthWorkoutSession.vue: completeCurrentSet persists values only through the explicit completion API
frontend/src/views/StrengthWorkoutSession.vue: onMounted loads saved session state; localStorage usage currently concerns rest sound
docs/sprints/sprint-36-first-party-strength-workout-tracking.md: durable completed sets and live session runner
acceptance_criteria: Editing reps or weight, switching to another set, and returning restores the unfinished values for the original set without changing the other set.
Reloading the same active workout restores the draft with a clear Not logged label; no completion request is sent automatically.
Successful logging or explicit discard clears that set draft; failed logging preserves it for retry.
Completed, abandoned, deleted, or server-updated sets do not silently receive stale draft values; conflicts offer an explicit review or discard choice.
Unavailable browser storage does not prevent logging; explain that draft recovery is unavailable. Tests use synthetic workout data and cover navigation, reload, failed saves, and stale drafts.

ideas.title: Reopen last week’s specialist advice
ideas.problem: AI team reports are saved under a week-specific settings key, but get_analysis always derives the current week. The Completed weeks view renders SundayReview, which reads the separate weekly-review history. Once the calendar advances, the inspected UI has no way to reopen an older saved specialist report and its HEAD COACH synthesis, even though that report remains stored.
ideas.proposal: Extend Completed weeks with a clearly labeled list of saved specialist analyses alongside existing Sunday summaries. Add bounded read-only list and week-detail endpoints and a shareable selected-week URL. Render the original stored report with its generation time and through-date; do not regenerate it or combine it with present-day recovery context. For older reports without saved citation labels, show honest unavailable-evidence states rather than inventing historical context.
ideas.benefit: Revisit the advice and tradeoffs you were given before deciding whether a training change helped, without spending another AI run.
evidence: backend/app/services/team_analysis.py: read_saved_analysis and save_analysis use team_analysis:{week} keys; get_analysis derives only the current week
backend/app/routers/coaching.py: GET /coaching/team-analysis exposes no historical week parameter or listing
docs/specs/001-hybrid-coaching-team/plan.md: per-week AI persistence and separate completed Sunday history
acceptance_criteria: With synthetic saved analyses for two weeks, both appear in a bounded history list and each can be reopened through a selected-week URL.
Opening a historical report uses its saved specialist text, HEAD COACH synthesis, generation timestamp and through-date, with no AI request or plan write.
Sunday summaries remain available and are clearly distinguished from specialist analyses, including weeks with only one report type.
Missing or deleted supporting activities are labeled unavailable; current recovery or profile data is never silently inserted into historical advice.
Invalid weeks, missing reports, empty history and API failures have clear states; tests cover Monday rollover and verify stored reports remain unchanged.

ideas.title: Find exercises for the equipment you have
ideas.problem: The Workout Studio exercise explorer supports muscle selection, name search and supporting-muscle inclusion, but cannot narrow results by available equipment. The new exercise-guide catalog already contains equipment metadata, so users currently need to inspect individual guides to find movements compatible with their gym or home setup.
ideas.proposal: Add an optional equipment filter to the existing exercise explorer, using explicitly mapped equipment requirements from the guide catalog. Keep the unfiltered list as the default and label exercises with unknown requirements separately. Combine equipment selection with the current muscle and name filters. This is a browsing aid: adding an exercise remains explicit and does not replace an existing movement or transfer its load prescription.
ideas.benefit: Build a workout more quickly when you have limited equipment or a preferred station, without opening every exercise guide.
evidence: frontend/src/components/StrengthExerciseExplorer.vue: explorer-filters and matches currently use query and includeSupporting
frontend/src/activity-detail/exercise-library.mjs: filterExercises filters muscle membership and exercise name
frontend/src/activity-detail/exercise-guides.mjs: getExerciseGuide returns explicit equipment metadata for matched aliases
frontend/tests/exercise-guides.test.mjs: conservative alias matching leaves ambiguous exercise variants unmapped
acceptance_criteria: With no equipment filter, the existing results and ordering remain unchanged.
Equipment filtering composes with muscle selection, supporting-muscle inclusion and name search, with an accessible labeled control and accurate result count.
Exercises with multiple known requirements match only when all required items are available; bodyweight and unknown equipment have distinct states.
Unknown or ambiguously mapped exercises are labeled Equipment unknown and are never presented as verified matches; users can explicitly include or inspect them.
Browsing or changing filters never modifies a saved workout. Adding a movement uses the existing explicit draft action without assuming equivalent loads or automatically substituting exercises.
Synthetic filter tests cover combined requirements, unknown metadata, conservative aliases and reset behavior; keyboard and narrow-screen checks cover the controls and empty state.

ideas.title: Check coaching advice before changing its prompt
ideas.problem: The weekly coaching helper is changing from separate specialist calls to one consolidated call. The inspected helper tests use canned model responses and prompt-string assertions, while backend tests check validation, stale snapshots and persistence. These checks do not show whether a prompt revision improves the actual advice or loses important tradeoffs.
ideas.proposal: Create a small developer-only suite of wholly synthetic weekly snapshots and a review rubric. Support an explicit comparison run of a baseline and candidate prompt using the same scenarios and model configuration, with saved outputs displayed side by side. Start with missing evidence, competing sport goals, a single hard ride in an otherwise ordinary week, and incomplete cycling-power coverage. Separate deterministic schema/citation checks from human judgments about evidence use, tradeoffs, uncertainty and the single proposed change. Keep model runs opt-in and outside the ordinary offline test command.
ideas.benefit: Make coaching prompt changes faster to assess and catch plausible-sounding regressions before trying them on a real training week.
evidence: scripts/team_coaching_helper.py: team_prompt and run_review now produce all specialist reports and HEAD COACH synthesis in one call
scripts/test_team_coaching_helper.py: test_one_consolidated_call_and_one_save supplies a canned response; prompt tests assert text inclusion
backend/tests/test_team_analysis.py: tests cover persistence, stale input rejection, citations and output length rather than generated advice quality
backend/app/services/power_trends.py: build_cycling_power_coaching_context documents missing-coverage and all-time-record interpretation limits
docs/roadmaps/roadmap-v3.md: engineering track targets service/API contracts; a synthetic prompt comparison workflow would complement those checks
acceptance_criteria: At least four versioned synthetic snapshots cover the named scenarios and include a short expected-behavior rubric without prescribing exact wording or one mandatory training recommendation.
An offline command validates fixtures and stored output structure/citations without reading the application database, calling a model, or contacting the running app.

An explicit model comparison command uses only the selected synthetic fixtures, bounds the number of calls, and records prompt hash, model configuration, scenario ID and run timestamp for both outputs.

The comparison artifact shows baseline and candidate advice side by side, distinguishing mechanical failures from human review judgments; it makes no unsupported claim that a single sample proves quality.
The workflow never saves a coaching review or changes a plan. Ordinary tests cannot trigger paid model runs, and a failed comparison preserves previously saved comparison artifacts.

ideas.title: Ride structured workouts in Zwift straight from the plan
ideas.problem: Recent riding is dominated by unstructured Zwift pacer group rides: the 28-day intensity focus is about 73% low aerobic and 3% anaerobic, with no hard sessions in the latest week. Planned ride days carry only an intent and a duration, so there is no concrete interval prescription to execute or judge afterwards.
ideas.proposal: Add a deterministic library of structured cycling workouts (recovery, endurance, tempo, sweet spot, threshold, VO2 max) defined as FTP-relative steps. Let a planned ride day reference a library workout, show its steps with watt targets from the stored FTP, and export it as a Zwift .zwo file. Expose the library through MCP so the planner can assign workouts.
ideas.benefit: Turn intended quality sessions into rides you can start in Zwift in one step, with targets that scale to your Zwift FTP.
evidence: backend/app/models/plans.py: WeeklyPlanDay has intent and duration but no workout structure
acceptance_criteria: Each library workout has an ID, intent, total duration and FTP-relative steps.
A planned ride day can reference a workout and the Plan view shows its steps and a .zwo download.
Exported .zwo files use FTP fractions so Zwift scales them to its own FTP setting.
Watt targets in the app state which stored FTP and date they use.
The library is readable through MCP; unknown workout IDs are rejected.

ideas.title: Notice when training volume quietly slides
ideas.problem: Weekly minutes fell from 706 to 457 to 342 over three consecutive weeks and fitness drifted down from mid-August, but no surface calls out a multi-week decline unless you read the charts yourself.
ideas.proposal: Detect two or three consecutive weeks of falling volume or fitness that do not match a planned lighter week. Show one compact dashboard alert that asks whether it was planned or life-driven, store the answer, and pass it into weekly coaching context.
ideas.benefit: Catch unplanned detraining early and let coaching distinguish a deliberate deload from a stressful stretch.
acceptance_criteria: The alert triggers on a documented rule over completed weeks only.
Weeks planned as lighter do not trigger it.
The athlete can label the drop as planned, life or illness/injury, and the label reaches coaching context.
No alert is shown when data coverage is insufficient.

ideas.title: Three-tap morning check-in including stress
ideas.problem: Subjective state is only recorded as post-activity feedback, so readiness goes stale (the latest check-in is a week old) and nothing captures life stress or sleep, which currently affect training more than load does.
ideas.proposal: Add a daily check-in, independent of activities, with energy, soreness, stress and sleep quality plus an optional pain/niggle score. Make it reachable in a few taps from mobile. Feed it into readiness so high-stress days bias toward easier sessions.
ideas.benefit: Keep readiness current and let the plan respond to stressful days without requiring a hard test or a completed workout.
acceptance_criteria: One check-in per day can be saved and edited without an activity.
Readiness uses the latest check-in and reports when it is missing or stale.
High stress or poor sleep produces visible, conservative guidance rather than silent plan changes.
The check-in fits a 390px viewport and is completable in three taps plus submit.

ideas.title: Suggest an FTP estimate without a test
ideas.problem: The stored FTP is 242 W from March and drives power-based training load, zones and workout targets. A maximal test is not appealing during a stressful period, and recent best efforts come from submaximal group rides, so a guessed value would be no better.
ideas.proposal: Compute a transparent FTP estimate from recent measured power (e.g. best efforts and sustained steady work) with the rides it came from and an explicit uncertainty note. Flag when the stored FTP is old or clearly inconsistent. Never write the estimate automatically; the athlete decides whether to log it.
ideas.benefit: Keep load and workout targets honest without forcing a maximal test.
acceptance_criteria: The estimate cites the efforts it uses and states that submaximal data can underestimate FTP.
A stale-FTP flag appears when the stored value is older than a documented threshold.
No FTP metric is created without an explicit user action.
Insufficient recent power data yields an unavailable state, not a number.

ideas.title: Recovery days that keep the streak and count as rest
ideas.problem: The daily streak is a deliberate goal and planning notes forbid rest days, while readiness flags seven active days out of seven as a risk. The planner already schedules easy sessions, but load and readiness do not treat a genuine recovery day differently from any other session.
ideas.proposal: Define a recovery day by a documented cap (e.g. a short walk, mobility or Z1 spin under a load threshold). Such days extend the streak, count toward rest in readiness and fatigue reads, and are proposed by the planner when fatigue or stress is elevated.
ideas.benefit: Protect the long streak without letting it block real recovery.
acceptance_criteria: Recovery-day criteria are documented and deterministic.
A qualifying day keeps the streak and is not counted as a training day in readiness.
Planned recovery days show the cap they must stay under.
Exceeding the cap is visible after the fact without breaking the streak.

ideas.title: Use one weekly strength target everywhere
ideas.problem: The active process goal and planning notes target three strength sessions per week, but the strength consistency summary uses a hard-coded target of two, so weeks can look hit on one surface and missed on another.
ideas.proposal: Derive the consistency target from the active strength-frequency goal when one exists, falling back to the current default otherwise.
ideas.benefit: See one consistent answer about whether a strength week counted.
acceptance_criteria: With an active strength-frequency goal, consistency uses its target.
Without one, the previous default is used.
A test covers both cases.

ideas.title: Structured return-to-run progression
ideas.problem: Running rules (reintroduce only while heel symptoms stay stable; never raise pace and distance in the same week) live only in free-text planning notes, and run heart rate averages are high for base rebuilding.
ideas.proposal: Track run-specific heel pain after each run and the next morning, a staged progression, a check that blocks raising pace and distance in one week, and an easy-run heart-rate cap. Park until running becomes a focus again.
ideas.benefit: Rebuild running confidently when the focus shifts back from cycling.
acceptance_criteria: Progression stage and heel scores are visible per run.
A plan that raises both pace and distance in one week is flagged before saving.
Easy runs above the heart-rate cap are marked in execution quality.

ideas.title: Correct the reason you gave for a quieter week
ideas.problem: The new volume alert hides its entire component after a reason is saved. Although the service supports updating the week-specific label, the inspected frontend exposes no control for revisiting that answer. An accidental tap can therefore leave an incorrect reason in coaching context.
ideas.proposal: Keep a compact saved-answer row for the currently evaluated volume-drop week, showing its date range and chosen reason with a Change action. Reuse the existing label endpoint to correct the same week explicitly. Keep the full warning dismissed after a successful save and show an inline retry state if a correction fails. This is a correction path for the existing alert, not another alert system.
ideas.benefit: Let the athlete fix an accidental answer quickly and keep coaching context aligned with what they meant.
evidence: frontend/src/components/VolumeTrendAlert.vue: root v-if requires trend.alert; label emits the response that hides the component
backend/app/services/volume_trend.py: build_volume_trend returns the saved label with alert false for a labeled sliding window
backend/app/services/volume_trend.py: save_volume_trend_label updates the same week on conflict
frontend/src/views/Dashboard.vue: onVolumeTrendLabeled replaces the dashboard trend
backend/tests/test_volume_trend.py: test_label_hides_alert_and_is_reported covers dismissal but not a visible correction path
acceptance_criteria: After saving a reason for a synthetic sliding week, the full alert disappears and a compact row shows the saved reason, evaluated week and a keyboard-accessible Change action.
Changing the reason updates the same week through the existing endpoint; a reload and coaching-context read return the corrected reason.
A failed correction preserves the last confirmed answer and offers retry without showing an unsaved choice as persisted.
Refreshing into a different evaluated week cannot send a pending correction to that new week; the user is asked to reopen the relevant current control.
Synthetic UI checks cover saving, correction, failed saves and reload at desktop and 390px widths. Merely opening the control never writes an answer.

ideas.title: See aerobic fitness improve without a test
ideas.problem: Aerobic progress during a cycling base block is invisible unless you do a maximal test, which you are avoiding for now. Power records only move on hard efforts, so steady endurance rides produce no fitness signal.
ideas.proposal: For steady rides of 45 minutes or more with power and heart rate, compute heart-rate drift (Pw:HR decoupling between the first and second halves) and efficiency (average power per heartbeat at endurance intensity). Show an 8–12 week trend on Cycling power with the qualifying rides listed, and let the coach say things like 'same power, 6 bpm lower than in August'.
ideas.benefit: Lets you watch indoor winter base fitness improve from normal Zone 2 rides, with no test and no extra fatigue.
acceptance_criteria: Only rides that meet documented steadiness, duration and data-completeness rules qualify; others are listed as excluded with a reason.
Each trend point links to its ride and shows decoupling percent and power-per-heartbeat.
Indoor and outdoor rides can be compared separately.
Fewer than three qualifying rides in the window yields an unavailable state, not a trend line.
Coach context receives a compact summary and no FTP is written.

ideas.title: Know when shoes, chain and tyres are worn out
ideas.problem: Worn-out run shoes are a common, silent injury risk, and your heel history makes this matter as running returns. Chains and tyres also wear on a schedule nobody remembers.
ideas.proposal: Add a small kit list (shoes, bike, chain, tyres, trainer) with a start date and replacement threshold. Assign kit to activities automatically by sport, with a manual override, using Strava gear where it exists. Show distance used and a calm 'nearly due' cue on Today and in the return-to-run panel.
ideas.benefit: Replace shoes before they cost you a heel flare-up, and stop guessing how old your chain is.
acceptance_criteria: Kit items can be created, retired and given a distance or time threshold.
New runs and rides are assigned to the default kit for their sport, and the assignment can be changed.
Accumulated distance updates when activities are added, deleted or reassigned.
Items at 90% of threshold show a nearly-due cue; retired items keep their history.

ideas.title: Train toward a target event with a countdown and taper
ideas.problem: Seasons and goals describe months and totals, but nothing models a specific day you want to be fresh for: a gran fondo, a 10K or a spring sportive. The planner cannot taper or build toward a date.
ideas.proposal: Let you set one A-event (and optional B-events) with date, sport and type. Show a countdown with the current phase (base, build, peak, taper, recovery) derived from weeks remaining. Give the planner and coach the phase so the last 7–14 days reduce volume while keeping some intensity, and add a race-week checklist (fuelling plan, kit check, travel).
ideas.benefit: Gives the long streak a destination, and makes sure you arrive at the event fresh rather than tired.
acceptance_criteria: An event can be created, edited and removed; at most one A-event is active.
The phase is computed deterministically from weeks remaining and is visible on Today and Plan.
Planning context includes the phase, and taper weeks show a reduced-volume target.
After the event date, the countdown is replaced by a recovery week prompt and the event is kept in history.

ideas.title: Suggest life-load tags from your calendar
ideas.problem: Life-load tags only work if you remember to add them. Busy days, travel and late events are usually already in your calendar.
ideas.proposal: Read the local macOS calendar for the coming week (read-only, on this machine only) and suggest life-load tags for crowded days, travel and late evenings. Show suggestions next to the plan for one-click accept or ignore; never tag automatically or send event titles to the AI coach.
ideas.benefit: The planner keeps hard sessions off chaotic days without you entering your schedule twice.
acceptance_criteria: Calendar access is opt-in and can be turned off; without access the feature is hidden.
Suggestions show the reason (e.g. '6 h of events', 'travel') but store no event titles.
Only accepted suggestions become life-load tags.
Coaching context receives tags only, never raw calendar data.

ideas.title: Add your own voice to the weekly review
ideas.problem: The HEAD COACH weekly review is built from data. It cannot know what felt good, what was hard emotionally, or what next week looks like, unless you write it into a planning brief separately.
ideas.proposal: Before generating the Sunday review, ask three optional questions: best moment, hardest moment, and anything coming up next week. Save the answers with the week and include them in the review and next week's planning context. Show your own words at the top of the saved review.
ideas.benefit: Reviews and plans reflect how training actually felt, and you build a journal of your season for free.
acceptance_criteria: All three questions are optional; skipping still generates the review.
Answers are saved per week and editable after the review is generated.
Saved reviews display the athlete's answers separately from coach text.
Next week's planning context includes the 'coming up' answer.

ideas.title: A short monthly letter from your coach
ideas.problem: Weekly reviews are detailed but short-sighted. Month-scale wins such as new records, streak milestones, sleep trends and goal progress are spread across pages and easy to miss.
ideas.proposal: On the first days of each month, offer a one-click letter covering the previous month: three wins (records, streak, consistency), one pattern noticed (from what-worked memory, sleep debt or life load) and one focus for next month. Keep a list of past letters.
ideas.benefit: A motivating look back that shows progress the weekly view hides, and one clear focus for the month ahead.
acceptance_criteria: Generation is explicit (one click), never automatic.
Wins cite the underlying records or numbers, with links.
Past letters are listed by month and stay unchanged once saved.
A month with little data produces a short honest letter rather than invented wins.
